questions.question_text: The point P (-2, -5) lies on the curve with equation y = f(x), x is an element of R. Find the point to which P is mapped, when the curve with equation y = f(x) is transformed to the curve with equation (a) y = f(x) + 2 (1 mark) (b) y = |f(x)| (1 mark) (c) y = 3f(x - 2) + 2 (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: (-2, -3). (1 mark)
(b) B1: (-2, 5). (1 mark)
(c) M1: Finds either coordinate, e.g. x = 0 or y = -13. A1: Correct coordinates (0, -13). (2 marks)

questions.question_text: f(x) = (x - 4)(x^2 - 3x + k) - 42, where k is a constant. Given that (x + 2) is a factor of f(x), find the value of k. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Sets f(-2) = 0, leading to an equation in k: (-2-4)((-2)^2 - 3(-2) + k) - 42 = 0. M1: Simplifies to a linear equation in k, -6(k+10) = 42, and solves it. A1: k = -17. (3 marks)

questions.question_text: A circle has equation x^2 + y^2 - 10x + 16y = 80. (a) Find (i) the coordinates of the centre of the circle, (ii) the radius of the circle. (3 marks) Given that P is the point on the circle that is furthest away from the origin O, (b) find the exact length OP. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a)(i) M1: Completes the square on both x and y terms: (x-5)^2 + (y+8)^2 = 80 + 25 + 64 = 169. A1: Centre (5, -8). (ii) A1: Radius 13. (3 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts sqrt(5^2 + 8^2) + 13, i.e. distance from origin to centre plus the radius. A1ft: OP = 13 + sqrt(89) (exact), following through on their centre and radius. (2 marks)

questions.question_text: (a) Express lim (as delta x -> 0) of the sum from x = 2.1 to x = 6.3 of (2/x) delta x, as an integral. (1 mark) (b) Hence show that lim (as delta x -> 0) of the sum from x = 2.1 to x = 6.3 of (2/x) delta x = ln k, where k is a constant to be found. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: States the integral from x=2.1 to x=6.3 of (2/x) dx, with correct limits and dx included. (1 mark)
(b) M1: Uses the integral of (2/x) dx = 2 ln x and applies the limits: [2 ln x] from 2.1 to 6.3 = 2 ln 6.3 - 2 ln 2.1. A1: CSO, proceeds (without resorting to rounded decimals) to ln 9, so k = 9. (2 marks)

questions.question_text: The height, h metres, of a tree, t years after being planted, is modelled by the equation h^2 = at + b, 0 <= t < 25, where a and b are constants. Given that: the height of the tree was 2.60 m, exactly 2 years after being planted; the height of the tree was 5.10 m, exactly 10 years after being planted; (a) find a complete equation for the model, giving the values of a and b to 3 significant figures. (4 marks) Given that the height of the tree was 7 m, exactly 20 years after being planted, (b) evaluate the model, giving reasons for your answer. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts to use h^2 = at + b with t=2, h=2.6 (or t=10, h=5.1) to form one correct equation, e.g. 2a+b=6.76. A1: Both correct equations 2a+b=6.76 and 10a+b=26.01. dM1: Solves the simultaneous equations to find a and b. A1: Full model h^2 = 2.41t + 1.95 (a = 2.41, b = 1.95, to 3sf). (4 marks)
(b) M1: Substitutes t=20 into the model to find h (or h^2), or substitutes h=7 to find t. A1: Compares the model's value (h = awrt 7.08 m, or t = awrt 19.5 years) with the given true value and draws a valid conclusion (e.g. 'good model' because the values are close). (2 marks)
questions.notes: Modelling context uses h^2 = at+b, which is solved as a pair of simultaneous linear equations in a and b -- tagged under algebra-factor-theorem for the simultaneous equations method; no better-fitting topic exists in the fixed vocabulary.

questions.question_text: Figure 1 shows a sketch of a curve C with equation y = f(x) where f(x) is a cubic expression in x. The curve passes through the origin, has a maximum turning point at (2, 8), has a minimum turning point at (6, 0). (a) Write down the set of values of x for which f'(x) < 0. (1 mark) The line with equation y = k, where k is a constant, intersects C at only one point. (b) Find the set of values of k, giving your answer in set notation. (2 marks) (c) Find the equation of C. You may leave your answer in factorised form. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: 2 < x < 6. (1 mark)
(b) M1: States either k > 8 or k < 0. A1: Fully correct set notation {k : k > 8} union {k : k < 0}. (2 marks)
(c) M1: Realises the equation of C has the form y = ax(x-6)^2 (double root at the minimum turning point x=6, single root at the origin x=0). dM1: Substitutes (2,8) into y = ax(x-6)^2 to find the value of a. A1: y = (1/4)x(x-6)^2. (3 marks)

questions.question_text: (i) Given that p and q are integers such that pq is even, use algebra to prove by contradiction that at least one of p or q is even. (3 marks) (ii) Given that x and y are integers such that x < 0 and (x + y)^2 < 9x^2 + y^2, show that y > 4x. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(i) B1: Sets up the contradiction using correct language: assumes/lets pq be even but both p and q are odd. M1: Uses a correct algebraic form for p and q with different variables, e.g. p=2m+1 and q=2n+1, and attempts to multiply them out. A1*: Obtains pq = (2m+1)(2n+1) = 4mn+2m+2n+1 = 2(2mn+m+n)+1, states this is odd, giving a contradiction, so at least one of p and q must be even. (3 marks)
(ii) M1: From (x+y)^2 < 9x^2+y^2, expands and simplifies to a correct intermediate line, e.g. 2xy < 8x^2. A1*: Since x<0, divides/rearranges correctly (with the inequality reversing at the correct point, and a correct reason given for the reversal) to reach y > 4x. (2 marks)

questions.question_text: Figure 2 shows a graph of the speed of a car, v ms^-1, as it travels between two sets of traffic lights. A car stops at two sets of traffic lights. The car takes T seconds to travel between the two sets of traffic lights. The speed of the car is modelled by the equation v = (10 - 0.4t) ln(t + 1), 0 <= t <= T, where t seconds is the time after the car leaves the first set of traffic lights. According to the model, (a) find the value of T. (1 mark) (b) show that the maximum speed of the car occurs when t = 26/(1 + ln(t + 1)) - 1. (4 marks) Using the iteration formula t_(n+1) = 26/(1 + ln(t_n + 1)) - 1, with t_1 = 7, (c)(i) find the value of t_3 to 3 decimal places, (ii) find, by repeated iteration, the time taken for the car to reach maximum speed. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: T = 25 (seconds). (1 mark)
(b) M1: Attempts to differentiate v = (10 - 0.4t) ln(t+1) using the product rule. A1: Correct derivative dv/dt = (10-0.4t)/(t+1) - 0.4 ln(t+1). dM1: Sets dv/dt = 0 and rearranges towards an equation where t occurs only once outside the ln term. A1*: Proceeds to the given answer t = 26/(1+ln(t+1)) - 1, showing all key steps. (4 marks)
(c)(i) M1: Applies the iteration formula at least once, e.g. t_2 = 26/(1+ln8) - 1 = awrt 7.44. A1: t_3 = awrt 7.298 (3dp). (ii) A1: Continues the iteration until the value converges, giving awrt 7.33 seconds (units required). (3 marks)

questions.question_text: Figure 3 shows a sketch of a parallelogram PQRS. Given that vector PQ = 2i + 3j - 4k and vector QR = 5i - 2k, (a) show that parallelogram PQRS is a rhombus. (2 marks) (b) Find the exact area of the rhombus PQRS. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts both |PQ|^2 = 2^2+3^2+(-4)^2 and |QR|^2 = 5^2+(-2)^2. A1: Shows |PQ| = |QR| = sqrt(29), so PQRS is a rhombus (two adjacent sides of the parallelogram are equal in length). (2 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts both diagonal vectors PR = PQ + QR = 7i+3j-6k and QS = -PQ + PS = 3i-3j+2k. A1: Both correct. dM1: Uses a correct method for the area of a rhombus from its diagonals, Area = (1/2)|PR||QS|. A1: Area = sqrt(517). (4 marks)

questions.question_text: A scientist is studying the number of bees and the number of wasps on an island. The number of bees, measured in thousands, Nb, is modelled by the equation Nb = 45 + 220 e^(0.05t), where t is the number of years from the start of the study. According to the model, (a) find the number of bees at the start of the study. (1 mark) (b) show that, exactly 10 years after the start of the study, the number of bees was increasing at a rate of approximately 18 thousand per year. (3 marks) The number of wasps, measured in thousands, Nw, is modelled by the equation Nw = 10 + 800 e^(-0.05t), where t is the number of years from the start of the study. When t = T, according to the models, there are an equal number of bees and wasps. (c) Find the value of T to 2 decimal places. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: 265 (thousand). (1 mark)
(b) M1: Differentiates to get dNb/dt = 11 e^(0.05t). M1: Substitutes t=10 into their derivative. A1*: dNb/dt = awrt 18.1, which is approximately 18 thousand per year. (3 marks)
(c) M1: Sets 45+220e^(0.05t) = 10+800e^(-0.05t) and multiplies/rearranges to remove the negative exponential term, e.g. 220e^(0.05t)+35-800e^(-0.05t)=0. A1: Correct quadratic in e^(0.05t): 220(e^(0.05t))^2 + 35e^(0.05t) - 800 = 0. M1: Solves the quadratic for e^(0.05t) = 1.829 (rejecting the negative root -1.988), then takes logs: 0.05t = ln(1.829). A1: T = awrt 12.08. (4 marks)

questions.question_text: Figure 4 shows a sketch of part of the curve C1 with equation y = 2x^3 + 10 (x > 0) and part of the curve C2 with equation y = 42x - 15x^2 - 7. (a) Verify that the curves intersect at x = 1/2. (2 marks) The curves intersect again at the point P. (b) Using algebra and showing all stages of working, find the exact x coordinate of P. (5 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Substitutes x=1/2 into both y=2x^3+10 and y=42x-15x^2-7 and finds the y-values. A1*: Both give y = 41/4, so the curves intersect at x=1/2 (given answer; conclusion required). (2 marks)
(b) M1: Sets 42x-15x^2-7 = 2x^3+10 and rearranges to the cubic 2x^3+15x^2-42x+17=0. dM1: Deduces (2x-1) is a factor (since x=1/2 is a root) and attempts to divide/factorise. A1: 2x^3+15x^2-42x+17 = (2x-1)(x^2+8x-17). M1: Solves x^2+8x-17=0 using a suitable method. A1: x = -4 + sqrt(33) only (the root x = -4 - sqrt(33) must not be included in the final answer). (5 marks)

questions.question_text: In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying on calculator technology are not acceptable. Show that the integral from 1 to e^2 of x^3 ln x dx = a*e^8 + b, where a and b are rational constants to be found. (5 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Integrates by parts the right way round: integral of x^3 ln x dx = (x^4/4) ln x - integral of (x^4/4)(1/x) dx. M1: Uses a correct method to integrate (x^4/4)(1/x) to give x^4/16. A1: integral of x^3 ln x dx = (x^4/4) ln x - x^4/16 (+c). M1: Substitutes the limits 1 and e^2 into an expression of this form, subtracts, and uses ln(e^2)=2. A1: Answer = (7/16)e^8 + 1/16, so a = 7/16 and b = 1/16. (5 marks)

questions.question_text: (i) In an arithmetic series, the first term is a and the common difference is d. Show that Sn = (n/2)[2a + (n-1)d]. (3 marks) (ii) James saves money over a number of weeks to buy a printer that costs £64. He saves £10 in week 1, £9.20 in week 2, £8.40 in week 3 and so on, so that the weekly amounts he saves form an arithmetic sequence. Given that James takes n weeks to save exactly £64, (a) show that n^2 - 26n + 160 = 0. (2 marks) (b) Solve the equation n^2 - 26n + 160 = 0. (1 mark) (c) Hence state the number of weeks James takes to save enough money to buy the printer, giving a brief reason for your answer. (1 mark)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(i) B1: Writes Sn = a + (a+d) + ... + (a+(n-1)d) (at least 3 correct terms including the first and last, with no extra incorrect terms). M1: Reverses the series and adds the two versions of Sn term by term to reach 2Sn = n(2a+(n-1)d). A1*: Proceeds to Sn = (n/2)[2a+(n-1)d] (given answer). (3 marks)
(ii)(a) M1: Sets up a correct equation using S=64, a=10, d=-0.8 in the sum formula, e.g. 64 = (n/2)(2x10+(n-1)x(-0.8)). A1*: Proceeds without error, expanding and rearranging, to n^2-26n+160=0 (given answer). (2 marks)
(b) B1: n = 10, 16. (1 mark)
(c) B1: States 10 weeks, with a minimal correct reason (e.g. he has already saved enough by week 10 so would not save for another 6 weeks; or by week 16 he would be saving negative amounts each week, which doesn't make sense). (1 mark)

questions.question_text: In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable. (a) Given that 2 sin(x - 60 degrees) = cos(x - 30 degrees), show that tan x = 3 sqrt(3). (4 marks) (b) Hence or otherwise solve, for 0 <= theta < 180 degrees, 2 sin 2theta = cos(2theta + 30 degrees), giving your answers to one decimal place. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Uses both compound angle expansions sin(x-60) = sinx cos60 - cosx sin60 and cos(x-30) = cosx cos30 + sinx sin30 to set up an equation in sinx and cosx. A1: Correct equation 2sinx cos60 - 2cosx sin60 = cosx cos30 + sinx sin30. M1: Uses sinx/cosx = tanx (or substitutes exact trig values, with at least two correct) and collects terms in sinx and cosx (or tanx). A1*: Proceeds to the given answer tanx = 3sqrt(3), showing all key steps. (4 marks)
(b) B1: Deduces that x = 2theta + 60 degrees (by comparing 2sin2theta=cos(2theta+30) with the identity from (a)). M1: Proceeds from tan(2theta+60)=3sqrt(3) to 2theta+60 = 79.1 degrees, 259.1 degrees (one correct value). dM1: Correct method to find one value of theta from their 2theta+60, e.g. theta = (79.1-60)/2. A1: theta = awrt 9.6 degrees, 99.6 degrees, with no other values in the range. (4 marks)

questions.question_text: A company makes toys for children. Figure 5 shows the design for a solid toy shaped like a piece of cheese. The toy is modelled so that: face ABC is a sector of a circle with radius r cm and centre A; angle BAC = 0.8 radians; faces ABC and DEF are congruent; edges AD, CF and BE are perpendicular to faces ABC and DEF; edges AD, CF and BE have length h cm. Given that the volume of the toy is 240 cm^3, (a) show that the surface area of the toy, S cm^2, is given by S = 0.8r^2 + 1680/r, making your method clear. (4 marks) Using algebraic differentiation, (b) find the value of r for which S has a stationary point. (4 marks) (c) Prove, by further differentiation, that this value of r gives the minimum surface area of the toy. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Sets up an allowable equation using volume = 240, e.g. (1/2) r^2 * 0.8h = 240 => h = 600/r^2. A1: correct h. dM1: attempts to substitute their h into S = 2*(1/2 r^2 * 0.8) + 2rh + 0.8rh (i.e. the two sector faces plus the three rectangular faces). A1*: proceeds, with rigorous and careful reasoning, to S = 0.8r^2 + 2.8rh = 0.8r^2 + 2.8*(600/r^2) = 0.8r^2 + 1680/r (given answer, so working must be fully shown). (4 marks)
(b) M1: differentiates to get dS/dr = 1.6r - 1680/r^2. A1: correct derivative. dM1: sets dS/dr = 0 and rearranges to r^3 = 1050. A1: r = awrt 10.2. (4 marks)
(c) M1: attempts to substitute their positive r into d^2S/dr^2 = 1.6 + 3360/r^3. A1ft: d^2S/dr^2 > 0 (using their r), so S is a minimum (must refer to the sign and draw the conclusion for full marks). (2 marks)

questions.question_text: Figure 6 shows a sketch of the curve C with parametric equations x = 8 sin^2 t, y = 2 sin 2t + 3 sin t, 0 <= t <= pi/2. The region R, shown shaded in Figure 6, is bounded by C, the x-axis and the line with equation x = 4. (a) Show that the area of R is given by the integral from t=0 to t=a of (8 - 8 cos 4t + 48 sin^2 t cos t) dt, where a is a constant to be found. (5 marks) (b) Hence, using algebraic integration, find the exact area of R. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts y*(dx/dt) = (2sin2t+3sint) x 16sint cost, using dx/dt=16sint cost, and uses sin2t=2sint cost. A1: Correct expanded integrand in t, equivalent to 48sin^2 t cost + 16sin^2 2t (also seen as 24sint sin2t + 16sin^2 2t, or 48sin^2 t cost + 64sin^2 t cos^2 t). M1: Uses cos4t = 1-2sin^2 2t (i.e. 1-8sin^2 t cos^2 t) to rewrite the sin^2 2t term. A1*: Proceeds to the given integrand 8-8cos4t+48sin^2 t cost, showing all key steps. B1: Deduces a = pi/4 (from x=4 giving 8sin^2 t=4, so sint=1/sqrt(2), t=pi/4). (5 marks)
(b) M1: Integrates each term: integral of 8 dt = 8t, integral of -8cos4t dt = -2sin4t, and uses an appropriate method (e.g. substitution u=sint) to integrate 48sin^2 t cost dt. A1: 8t - 2sin4t + 16sin^3 t (+c). M1: Substitutes the limits a=pi/4 and 0 into their integrated expression, using exact trig values, to reach an exact answer. A1: CSO, Area = 2*pi + 4*sqrt(2) (or an equivalent exact form such as 2pi + sqrt(32)). (4 marks)
questions.notes: The raw PDF text badly scrambled the superscript placement in the integrand (rendered as 'sin t cos 2 t'). I reconstructed the correct term as 48*sin^2(t)*cos(t) (not sin(t)*cos^2(t)) by independently deriving y*(dx/dt) from the parametric equations and cross-checking against the mark scheme's part (b) antiderivative 16sin^3(t), which only arises from integrating sin^2(t)cos(t) (via u=sint), and against the final confirmed answer 2*pi+4*sqrt(2). Confidence in this reconstruction is high given the two independent checks, but flagging the reasoning here for transparency.
